Question: How can PtRu-based high-entropy alloys be synthesized with subnanometer dimensions and tailored morphologies to achieve high activity, stability, and CO resistance for alkaline hydrogen oxidation reaction (HOR)?. System: PtRuNiCoFeMo high-entropy alloy subnanometer nanowires (SNWs) with composition Pt/Ru/Ni/Co/Fe/Mo = 29.6/9.3/15.2/15.6/12.2/18.1 (SEM-EDS) or 28.5/6.8/18.6/15.2/10.7/20.2 (ICP-OES). Processing: Synthesis via solvothermal reduction: metal precursors (Pt(acac)2, Ru(acac)3, Ni(acac)2, Co(acac)3, Fe(acac)3, Mo(CO)6), glucose (reducing agent), and STAB (structure-directing agent) dissolved in oleylamine (OAm), heated at 210 °C for 5 h, followed by centrifugation and washing with cyclohexane/ethanol (1:9 v/v). Test conditions: Alkaline HOR in 0.1 M KOH solution purged with H2; accelerated durability test (ADT) for 2000 cycles between -0.1 V and 0.4 V vs. RHE at 500 mV s-1; CO poisoning tests in 0.1 M KOH with 1000 ppm CO/H2; chronoamperometry at 100 mV vs. RHE. Findings: Mass activity of HEA SNWs/C reached 6.75 A mgPt+Ru−1, which is 4.1 times higher than commercial PtRu/C (1.65 A mgPt+Ru−1) and 19.8 times higher than Pt/C (0.34 A mgPt+Ru−1); Specific activity of HEA SNWs/C was 8.96 mA cm−2, 2.4 times higher than PtRu/C (3.77 mA cm−2) and 18.7 times higher than Pt/C (0.48 mA cm−2); Only 6.2% loss in mass activity was observed after 2000 ADT cycles for HEA SNWs/C, compared to 20.6%, 31.5%, and 35.3% losses for HEA NPs/C, PtRu/C, and Pt/C respectively; In the presence of 1000 ppm CO, the limiting current density of HEA SNWs/C decreased by only 5.4% at 100 mV vs. RHE, whereas PtRu/C and Pt/C decreased by 21.3% and 22.7%; Chronoamperometry showed HEA SNWs/C activity decreased by 26.4% after 2000 s in 1000 ppm CO, while PtRu/C decreased by 82.9% and Pt/C completely deactivated after 1130 s; The d-band center of HEA SNWs/C shifted upwards to -3.835 eV compared to -3.732 eV for HEA NPs/C, weakening H* adsorption and facilitating OH* adsorption; DFT calculations revealed the energy barrier for H2O formation on HEA surface was as low as 0.08 eV, much lower than 0.57 eV for Pt and 0.27 eV for PtRu; The binding strength of H* on HEA SNWs/C was weakened to an appropriate level near 0 eV, while OH* binding on Ru was moderate at nearly -0.6 eV. Mechanism: Strong electronic interactions between different metal sites in HEA SNWs regulate the binding strength of protons and hydroxyls; Co and Ni sites maintain stable valence states due to pinning effects by Fe and Mo, while Pt and Ru sites modulate overall electroactivity; the upshifted d-band center weakens H* adsorption and facilitates OH* adsorption, and the low energy barrier for H2O formation (0.08 eV) enables rapid desorption and superior HOR activity. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that controlled synthesis of PtRu-based HEAs with tailored morphologies remains a general challenge in the field. Future work: The authors propose that the work provides a viable synthetic route for fabricating Pt-based HEA subnano/nano materials and promotes fundamental research on catalysis and beyond. Quote: "The mass and specific activities of HEA SNWs/C reach 6.75 A mgPt+Ru−1 and 8.96 mA cm−2, respectively"

card: Paper card. Question: How can oxygen defects in ceria nanocrystals be engineered for enhanced catalysis via a high-entropy oxide strategy?. System: Ceria-based nanocrystals with surface-confined atomic high-entropy oxide layers. Processing: Colloidal synthesis at 220 °C, followed by annealing in air at 500 °C. Test conditions: CO oxidation, temperature-programmed reduction, and oxygen isotope exchange. Findings: Introduction of transition-metal components to ceria enhances surface redox properties; Surface-confined atomic high-entropy oxide layers promote formation of surface oxygen vacancies; CuCoFeNiMn-CeO2 sample exhibits optimal CO oxidation capabilities; Enhanced configurational entropy facilitates activation of surface lattice oxygen; Surface oxygen vacancies are positively correlated with transition-metal substitution. Mechanism: The strong covalency of the transition-metal–oxygen bonds at the high-entropy oxide–ceria interface promotes the formation of surface oxygen vacancies, enabling efficient oxygen activation and replenishment for enhanced CO oxidation capabilities. Future work: More work is anticipated to unravel the metal–oxygen covalency in mixed and entropy-stabilized metal oxides. Quote: "The strong covalency of the transition-metal–oxygen bonds facilitates the formation of surface-confined oxygen vacancies"

card: Paper card. Question: How do the unique structural features of compositionally complex solid solutions (CCSS) enable new concepts in electrocatalyst design compared to traditional catalysts, and what are the strategies to exploit these features for activity, selectivity, and stability?. System: Compositionally complex solid solutions (CCSS) and high-entropy alloys (HEAs) defined as single-phase solid solutions with five or more elements, including specific examples like Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and Pd-based systems.. Processing: Synthesis via entropy-driven routes at high temperatures or high energies to ensure negative Gibbs free energy; non-equilibrium methods such as fast cooling rates (quenching) to kinetically trap metastable phases or achieve high deviations from equiatomic compositions (e.g., 60–70% of one element).. Test conditions: Electrochemical reactions including oxygen reduction reaction (ORR), oxygen evolution reaction (OER), hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), CO oxidation, CO reduction, CO2 reduction, NH3 synthesis/decomposition, MeOH oxidation, EtOH oxidation, and Li-O2 batteries.. Findings: CCSS materials form a single-phase solid solution where all elements are statistically distributed, creating millions of different multielement active sites with a continuous distribution of binding energies.; The binding energy distribution pattern (BEDP) for a quinary alloy shows at least five distinct binding peaks, with the position of the peak maximum related to overpotential and the integral related to the number of active sites.; Increasing the molar ratio of a specific element can increase the number of sites within a binding peak to about 60–70%, significantly surpassing the loss of site probability compared to unary catalysts.; In CCSS surfaces, the scaling relation between *O and *OH/*OOH is broken because *O binds at threefold hollow sites while *OH and *OOH bind at on-top sites with different elemental compositions.; For cascade reactions like CO2 reduction, the multifunctionality allows intermediate products to desorb and re-bind at different sites, enabling the synthesis of higher-carbon products.; The thermodynamic stability of the CCSS phase is counterbalanced by kinetic stabilization due to sluggish diffusion and high solid diffusion barriers, leading to high electrocatalytic stability.; The position of individual elements in standard volcano plots is not decisive; for example, Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni showed good ORR activity even though all individual elements are far from optimal volcano positions.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the immense flexibility in adjusting binding energies arises because every active site has a different elemental environment due to the statistical distribution of elements. This creates a continuous coverage of binding energies via BEDP peak broadening, allowing the formation of sites with ideal binding energies. Additionally, the unique multifunctionality allows different reaction steps or intermediates to bind at different sites, breaking traditional scaling relations and enabling cascade reactions.. Limitations: A lower abundance of relevant active sites on the surface compared to unary catalysts; the complexity of predicting suitable element combinations due to multielement interactions; challenges in synthesizing particles with controlled composition, size, and morphology; and the potential for thermodynamic degradation if the CCSS phase is metastable.. Future work: The authors propose developing a database summarizing calculated and experimental data, implementing high-throughput methods, using machine learning tools to identify trends in the complex composition space, and designing synthesis routes that allow upscaling to industrial scale while controlling electrochemical properties.. Quote: "Since the binding energy is a result of many short‐range and long‐range interactions of the binding atom(s) with all neighbouring atoms, an active site can consist of any possible arrangement of the constituent elements."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy be developed that exhibits superior radiation resistance compared to pure tungsten, specifically avoiding the formation of irradiation-induced dislocation loops under fusion-relevant conditions?. System: Quaternary W-Ta-Cr-V high-entropy alloy with atomic composition 38% W, 36% Ta, 15% Cr, and 11% V. Processing: Magnetron sputtering deposition from pure metal targets (99.99% purity) at room temperature and 3 mtorr pressure; deposition powers of 192 W (Cr), 312 W (V), 277 W (Ta), and 300 W (W) with 20 W bias radio frequency power; film thicknesses of ~100 nm for TEM and ~3 μm for mechanical testing. Test conditions: In situ irradiation with 1-MeV Kr+2 ions at 1073 K (dpa rates 0.0006 and 0.0016 dpa s−1) up to 8 dpa; ex situ irradiation with 3-MeV Cu+ ions at 773 K and 1050 K up to a peak dose of ~17 dpa; thermal annealing up to 1073 K; nanoindentation and nanoDMA testing. Findings: The as-deposited alloy exhibits a bimodal grain size distribution with ~70% of grains in the nanocrystalline regime (≤100 nm) and ultrafine regions (100 to 500 nm).; A unique 4-nm lamella-like compositional layering structure was revealed by atom probe tomography (APT) in the as-deposited state.; No irradiation-created dislocation loops were observed even after 8 dpa of irradiation at 1073 K.; Black spots observed after thermal annealing and irradiation were identified as Cr- and V-rich second-phase precipitates (~3 to 5 nm in size) rather than dislocation loops.; The as-deposited samples showed a hardness of 14 GPa with near negligible irradiation hardening.; Modeling predicts the formation of Cr- and V-rich precipitates due to negative enthalpies of mixing for W-Ta, W-V, and Cr-V binaries.; Theoretical modeling suggests equal mobilities of vacancies and self-interstitials are the origin of the exceptional radiation tolerance.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the exceptional radiation tolerance arises from the equal mobilities of point defects (vacancies and self-interstitials), which maximizes the recombination probability and minimizes defect clustering. This equal mobility is attributed to the rough energy landscape induced by local lattice distortion and chemical disparity in the high-entropy alloy. Additionally, the high density of grain boundaries acts as preferential recombination/annihilation sites for defects.. Limitations: The study was conducted on thin films rather than bulk materials; the exact mechanism for the equal defect mobilities is not fully elucidated beyond the correlation with the energy landscape; the procedure to distinguish precipitates from dislocation loops using TEM breaks down for asymmetric strain fields or non-edge dislocation loops.. Future work: The authors state that the suitability of these alloys for bulk production coupled with their exceptional radiation resistance makes them ideal structural materials for applications requiring extreme irradiation conditions, implying a need for bulk synthesis and further testing.. Quote: "No sign of irradiation-created dislocation loops, even after 8 dpa, was observed."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the synthesis of high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanocrystals be controlled and predicted to achieve specific structures and properties?. System: Quinary HEA nanocrystals made of platinum-group metals (Pd, Pt, Rh, Ir, and Ru). Processing: Dropwise synthesis with controlled reduction kinetics and entropy of mixing. Test conditions: Various reaction temperatures, precursor concentrations, and injection rates. Findings: The dropwise synthesis can manipulate a steady state for the number of each metal precursor at the same and different periods during the synthesis; Three distinctive types of HEA nanocrystals can be obtained: typical solid-solution PdPtRhIrRu nanocrystals, dendritic solid-solution PdPtRhIrRu nanocrystals, and Pd@PdPtRhIrRu core-shell nanocrystals; The dendritic solid-solution PdPtRhIrRu nanocrystals show greatly enhanced activity and durability toward hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and hydrogen oxidation reaction (HOR); The HEA-based nanocrystals exhibit high durability and retain their activities during accelerated durability tests. Mechanism: The formation of high-entropy solid-solution mixing induces a fine-tuning electronic structure of HEA nanocrystals, leading to a synergistic effect and enhanced catalytic activity. Future work: Further study to promote the interaction or synergistic effect between the multielement HEA support with a unique high-entropy coordination environment and the active component may greatly enhance the catalytic activity and thus high atomic efficiency. Quote: "Toward controllable and predictable synthesis of high-entropy alloy nanocrystals"

Processing: Vacuum arc melting (VAM), mechanical alloying (MA), spark plasma sintering (SPS), and magnetron sputtering (MS). Test conditions: High temperatures (up to 1200 °C), neutron irradiation, and corrosive environments (such as sulfuric acid and NaCl solution). Findings: The VCrFeTa0.1W0.1 and VCrFeTa0.2W0.2 RHEAs demonstrated improved hardness and exhibited a compressive yield strength exceeding 1000 MPa after annealing at 600 and 800 °C; The MoWAlCrTi RHEA showed excellent high-temperature oxidation resistance, with a specific mass change of only about 0.2 mg/(cm2·h) after exposure to air at 1000 °C for 40 h; The W0.5(TaTiVCr)0.5 RHEA exhibited excellent irradiation resistance, with only slight damage after He+ ion irradiation; The WNbMoTaV RHEA showed superior wear resistance, with a wear rate almost 80% lower than Inconel 718 using an Al ball under a 2000 m sliding distance. Mechanism: The excellent functional properties of W-containing RHEAs are attributed to the formation of dense oxide protective layers, passive films, and solid solution strengthening. Limitations: The number of reported W-containing RHEAs is far less than the theoretically predicted systems, and the effects of different elements on the phase structure, mechanical properties, and functional characteristics of RHEAs are not fully understood. Future work: Further research is necessary to develop new W-containing RHEA systems with high-end properties, to reveal the strengthening and deformation mechanisms of W-containing RHEAs in harsh environments, and to investigate the machining performance of W-containing RHEAs. card: Paper card. Question: How does the rapid solidification inherent to additive manufacturing (specifically SLM and DLF) influence phase selection, microstructure, and mechanical properties in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) compared to conventional processing methods?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) / Multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) defined as having at least five principal elements in equimolar/equiatomic compositions (5%–35% concentration each); specifically discussed in the context of bulk HEAs processed by SLM, SEBM, and DLF.. Processing: Additive manufacturing techniques including Selective Laser Melting (SLM), Selective Electron Beam Melting (SEBM), and Direct Laser Fabrication (DLF); DLF allows the use of elemental powders fed from different hoppers to produce in situ chemically homogeneous alloys, avoiding the need for pre-alloyed powders.. Test conditions: Not stated in the provided text; the text is a review summarizing published data rather than reporting new experimental test conditions for specific HEA samples.. Findings: HEAs are particularly well suited to AM, with the field expected to grow significantly in the coming years.; Laser-induced rapid solidification in AM can avoid compositional segregation and restrict the formation of brittle intermetallic compounds.; AM of HEAs allows the use of elemental powders as feedstock in DLF, avoiding the need for pre-alloyed metal powders.; Rapid solidification inherent to AM provides a tool to aid phase selection during alloy fabrication.; Traditionally, arc-melting requires extensive re-melting and intermittent ingot inversions, while SPS requires powder alloying and refinement via ball milling.; AM offers advantages over traditional methods by addressing shape and size limitations of HEA components.; The configurational entropy in HEAs stabilizes simple solid solutions (bcc, fcc, hcp), but competition with enthalpy often dictates the final microstructure.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the rapid solidification inherent to the AM process restricts the formation of brittle intermetallic compounds and avoids compositional segregation, while the high configurational entropy stabilizes simple solid solution phases. In DLF specifically, the mechanism involves the controlled supply of elemental powders from different hoppers to produce chemically homogeneous alloys in situ under optimized processing conditions.. Limitations: The text notes that AM of HEAs is a nascent field, stating that 'only two papers on SEBM and SLM' had been published at the time of writing, and that the properties obtained and effects of processing on microstructures are still being discussed.. Future work: The authors state that 'we may expect this field to grow significantly in the coming years' and that the properties and microstructural effects of AM on HEAs are currently being discussed, implying a need for further characterization of these relationships.. Quote: "The impact of rapid solidification inherent to AM on phase selection is highlighted for high-entropy alloys."

Paper card. Question: How does the use of LENS™ additive manufacturing influence the microstructure, phase constitution, and mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys compared to conventional casting, and can it enable the creation of compositionally graded materials?. System: Al1.5CoCrCuFeNi, ZrTiVCrFeNi, TiZrNbMoV, AlCoCrCuFeNiTi, AlCoCrFeNi, CoCrFeNi, AlxCoCrFeNi (x = 0.3, 0.6, 0.85), AlxFeCoCrNi(2-x) (x = 0.3, 1), AlxCuCrFeNi2 (0 < x < 1.5), AlCrSiTiV, Al2CoCrCuFeNi. Processing: Laser Engineered Net Shaping (LENS™) using powder-fed systems with elemental powder blends or pre-alloyed powders; Laser cladding with laser power 0.4–3 kW, beam size 0.6–4.5 mm, scanning velocity 1.7–12 mm/s, and effective energy 46–208 J/mm²; Selective Electron Beam Melting (SEBM) using gas-atomized powder; Selective Laser Melting (SLM) using gas-atomized powder. Test conditions: Compression testing, tensile testing, microhardness testing, magnetic property measurement (saturation magnetization and coercivity), dry sliding wear tests at room temperature and 500°C, hydrogen storage exposure, annealing exposure. Findings: LENS™ processing of Al1.5CoCrCuFeNi resulted in dendritic grains containing an ordered B2 structure and a disordered bcc matrix, avoiding the slow cooling and segregation typical of arc-melting.; ZrTiVCrFeNi and TiZrNbMoV alloys synthesized via LENS™ exhibited dendritic two-phase structures and performed well for hydrogen storage due to non-equilibrium solute-trapping effects.; SLM CoCrFeNi achieved a yield strength of 600 MPa, triple that of its cast equivalent (188 MPa), while maintaining high ductility (32% elongation).; SEBM-processed AlCoCrFeNi showed superior ductility (14%–26% elongation) compared to the as-cast state (5% elongation), attributed to grain refinement and the presence of an fcc phase.; In AlxCuCrFeNi2 graded deposits, microhardness increased progressively with Al content as the microstructure transitioned from fcc/L12 to bcc/B2.; Magnetic properties varied with Al content: low Al regions were weakly ferromagnetic, while high Al bcc/B2 regions were strongly ferromagnetic with high saturation magnetization.; Laser-cladded HEA coatings achieved room temperature hardness values exceeding ceramic particle-reinforced Mg-, Al-, and Ti-matrix alloys and Nb, Ta, and Mo alloys.; AlCrSiTiV clad coatings showed a friction coefficient of ~0.3 and specific wear rate of ~2.10⁻⁵ mm³/Nm, which were 2 and 3 times lower than the Ti-6Al-4V substrate, respectively.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the observed microstructural changes and property enhancements to the rapid cooling rates (10⁴–10⁶ K/s) inherent to laser-based additive manufacturing, which cause significant grain refinement, non-equilibrium solute-trapping, and the formation of non-equilibrium phases like bcc that are favored over fcc. The high temperature gradients and solidification rates control the columnar-to-equiaxed transition, while the high viscosity and sluggish diffusion rates of HEA melts limit dilution with substrates.. Limitations: The text notes that the statistical comparison of phases in laser-cladded coatings is biased because 90% of reported coatings contain Al, which stabilizes the bcc phase. Additionally, the presence of metallurgical defects, heterogeneity, and anisotropy in microstructures limits the use of these techniques for fracture applications, and durability properties like corrosion resistance and fracture toughness require further characterization.. Future work: The authors propose that systematic efforts must be made to characterize powder characteristics more finely and incorporate these into simulations. They suggest implementing tools to characterize materials in real-time during processing and using advanced techniques like synchrotron diffraction. Further focus should be devoted to evaluating microstructure and tensile properties to understand the mechanisms of microstructure development, and to exploring in situ thermal treatments to design multiphase steel architectures.. Quote: "The faster cooling rates obtained via direct laser metal deposition lead to a significant non-equilibrium solute-trapping effect, which in turn avoided the component segregation and relieved the solubility limitations."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a low-temperature, rapid single-source precursor approach be used to synthesize a phase-pure, high-entropy 2D hexernary transition metal dichalcogenide (MoWReMnCr)S2 that exhibits enhanced hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) activity compared to 2H-MoS2?. System: Hexernary high-entropy metal disulfide (MoWReMnCr)S2; 2H-MoS2 (control); 20% w/w carbon black (CB) composite. Processing: Tandem thermal decomposition of five equimolar metal dithiocarbamate precursors (MoL4, WS(S2)L2, Re2(µ–S)2(L)4, MnL3, CrL3) at 500 °C for 1 h under argon flow (300 cm3 min−1); followed by liquid-phase exfoliation (LPE) in N-methyl pyrrolidine for 24 h with ultrasonication (37 kHz, 30% power) and centrifugation (1500 rpm, 3 h). Test conditions: HER electrocatalysis in 0.5 M H2SO4 electrolyte; Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) at 5 mV s−1; Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) at −0.47 V vs Ag/AgCl; Chronopotentiometry at 10 mA cm−2 for 20 h; 7000-cycle CV stability test. Findings: The synthesized (MoWReMnCr)S2 contains 5.0 mol% Mn and 4.7 mol% Cr successfully incorporated into the 2H-MoS2 lattice, confirmed by pXRD and Raman spectroscopy.; Exfoliated nanosheets consist of 3–7 atomic layers with a homogeneous elemental distribution at the nanoscale, verified by HAADF-STEM and EDX mapping.; The (MoWReMnCr)S2@20%CB electrode achieved an overpotential of 229 ± 5 mV to reach 10 mA cm−2, significantly lower than the 362 mV for MoS2@20%CB.; The onset potential for (MoWReMnCr)S2@20%CB was −127 mV, compared to −219 mV for MoS2@20%CB.; The Tafel slope for (MoWReMnCr)S2 was 133.8 mV dec−1, indicating a Volmer-limited mechanism, compared to 152.9 mV dec−1 for MoS2.; Charge transfer resistance (Rct) for (MoWReMnCr)S2@20%CB was 3.12 Ω cm2, approximately eight times lower than the 25.11 Ω cm2 for MoS2@20%CB.; DFT calculations predicted that Cr and Mn substitutions activate the basal plane, reducing H adsorption energy (Eads) to near the optimal value of −0.24 eV.; The catalyst demonstrated high stability, retaining activity after 7000 CV cycles and 20 h of continuous operation at 10 mA cm−2.. Mechanism: The enhanced catalytic activity is attributed to the 'cocktail effect' where the high configurational entropy stabilizes the 2H phase and allows for the incorporation of Cr and Mn. DFT calculations suggest that substituting Mo with Cr and Mn activates the basal plane sites toward H adsorption, shifting the reaction mechanism to a Volmer-limited process with near-thermoneutral H adsorption energetics, while largely preserving the favorable electronic structure of MoS2.. Limitations: The study notes that the exfoliation process produced a size dispersion of nanosheets, and while purification to isolate monolayers is possible via liquid cascade centrifugation, it was beyond the scope of the current work. Additionally, the calculated electrochemically-active surface area (ECSA) using double-layer capacitance was deemed unreliable due to high frequency dispersion effects, requiring an alternative strategy using cyclic voltammetry.. Future work: The authors propose that the scalable synthesis approach is a universal route to produce 2D high-entropy materials of various transition-metal disulfides and that entropic stabilization of nanosheets is a powerful approach to produce 2D materials that cannot otherwise be produced due to intrinsic instability in the low-dimensional limit.. Quote: "A low‐temperature (500 °C) and rapid (1 h) single source precursor approach is successfully adopted to synthesize the hexernary high‐entropy metal disulfide (MoWReMnCr)S2."

card: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy alloy nanopatterns be synthesized using a DNA origami-based metallization reaction system?. System: High-entropy multimetallic nanopatterns composed of up to five metal elements (Co, Pd, Pt, Ag, and Ni). Processing: DNA origami-based metallization reaction system with a one-step or two-step process, using metal ion precursors and reducing agents. Test conditions: Room temperature, 1× TA–Mg2+ buffer, and various reducing agents. Findings: Multimetallic nanopatterns with controlled morphology, composition, and uniformity can be synthesized; The atomic distribution uniformity of multimetallic nanopatterns can be regulated by specific elements; The introduction of Ag leads to a decrease in catalytic activity, while the introduction of Ni leads to enhanced catalytic performance; The CoPdPt nanoalloy has the highest catalytic activity among the tested multimetallic nanoalloys; The KM value for H2O2 is 0.98 mM, indicating a higher affinity to the substrate than horseradish peroxidase. Mechanism: The strong coordination between metal elements and DNA bases enables the accumulation of metal ions on protruding clustered DNA (pcDNA), which serves as a nucleation site for metal plating. Limitations: The immiscible nature of some metal elements, such as Ag, can lead to phase separation and inhomogeneous distribution. Future work: Developing methodologies for uniformity and phase separation control, and exploring the potential of nanoalloys arrays with specific shapes and components for catalysis. Quote: "High-entropy multimetallic nanopatterns with controlled morphology, composition and uniformity hold great potential for developing nanoelectronics, nanophotonics and catalysis"
